fr:title.text: Well-foundedness of the Dyck functor via the string-decomposition axiom

fr:frontmatter.fr:title: Well-foundedness of the Dyck functor via the string-decomposition axiom

fr:mainmatter.html:p: Pre-meeting notes for the advisor meeting on 2026-04-22. Context: the well-foundedness sense here is the one in [alexandruIntrinsicallyCorrectAlgorithms2025-preprint], and the tie-in with well-founded recursive coalgebras in dep-Lambek is the reason for caring.
The Dyck functor. Consider the polynomial functor
and let D be its initial F-algebra, so D \simeq I \oplus \texttt {"}lp\texttt {"} \otimes D \otimes \texttt {"}rp\texttt {"} \otimes D.

The string-decomposition axiom. In dep-Lambek we have the axiom \top \simeq \mathchoice {\textstyle \oplus _{{\mathopen {}\left (w : \mathrm {String}\right )\mathclose {}}}}{\textstyle \oplus _{{\mathopen {}\left (w : \mathrm {String}\right )\mathclose {}}}}{\scriptstyle \oplus _{{\mathopen {}\left (w : \mathrm {String}\right )\mathclose {}}}}{\scriptscriptstyle \oplus _{{\mathopen {}\left (w : \mathrm {String}\right )\mathclose {}}}}\, \lceil w \rceil which internalizes the external reasoning on strings: every top-element is quoted as some specific w. Equivalently \top \simeq {\mathtt {Char}}^{*} \quad \text {where} \quad \mathtt {Char} = \mathchoice {\textstyle \oplus _{{\mathopen {}\left (c : \mathcal {A}\right )\mathclose {}}}}{\textstyle \oplus _{{\mathopen {}\left (c : \mathcal {A}\right )\mathclose {}}}}{\scriptstyle \oplus _{{\mathopen {}\left (c : \mathcal {A}\right )\mathclose {}}}}{\scriptscriptstyle \oplus _{{\mathopen {}\left (c : \mathcal {A}\right )\mathclose {}}}}\, \texttt {"}c\texttt {"}.

Decomposing D. Using the axiom we can refine D into an indexed sum over explicit sub-strings. Peeling off one constructor and inserting a quote for each recursive occurrence gives D \simeq I \oplus \mathchoice {\textstyle \oplus _{{\mathopen {}\left (w : \mathrm {String}\right )\mathclose {}}}}{\textstyle \oplus _{{\mathopen {}\left (w : \mathrm {String}\right )\mathclose {}}}}{\scriptstyle \oplus _{{\mathopen {}\left (w : \mathrm {String}\right )\mathclose {}}}}{\scriptscriptstyle \oplus _{{\mathopen {}\left (w : \mathrm {String}\right )\mathclose {}}}}\, \mathchoice {\textstyle \oplus _{{\mathopen {}\left ({\mathopen {}\left (w = \texttt {"}lp\texttt {"}\, w_1\, \texttt {"}rp\texttt {"}\, w_2\right )\mathclose {}}\right )\mathclose {}}}}{\textstyle \oplus _{{\mathopen {}\left ({\mathopen {}\left (w = \texttt {"}lp\texttt {"}\, w_1\, \texttt {"}rp\texttt {"}\, w_2\right )\mathclose {}}\right )\mathclose {}}}}{\scriptstyle \oplus _{{\mathopen {}\left ({\mathopen {}\left (w = \texttt {"}lp\texttt {"}\, w_1\, \texttt {"}rp\texttt {"}\, w_2\right )\mathclose {}}\right )\mathclose {}}}}{\scriptscriptstyle \oplus _{{\mathopen {}\left ({\mathopen {}\left (w = \texttt {"}lp\texttt {"}\, w_1\, \texttt {"}rp\texttt {"}\, w_2\right )\mathclose {}}\right )\mathclose {}}}}\, \texttt {"}lp\texttt {"} \otimes {\mathopen {}\left (\lceil w_1 \rceil \mathrel {\And } D\right )\mathclose {}} \otimes \texttt {"}rp\texttt {"} \otimes {\mathopen {}\left (\lceil w_2 \rceil \mathrel {\And } D\right )\mathclose {}}.

Because w = \texttt {"}lp\texttt {"}\, w_1\, \texttt {"}rp\texttt {"}\, w_2, we know |w_1|, |w_2| < |w|. The well-foundedness argument is now visible in the type: the recursive D occurrences are guarded by shorter quoted strings.

Reading. The string-decomposition axiom is doing all of the work of externally reasoning about string length. Everything that normally lives "on paper" — inducting on |w|, case-splitting on the first character — is now accessible internally through the quote types \lceil - \rceil and the \oplus /\mathrel {\And } structure. See also the trivial-case question for the related \top vs. \lceil w \rceil puzzle in the guarded setting.

fr:title.text: Candidates for a guarded modality in dep-Lambek

fr:frontmatter.fr:title: Candidates for a guarded modality in dep-Lambek

fr:mainmatter.html:p: Pre-meeting notes for the advisor meeting on 2026-04-22. Related: Can I use guarded recursion?, well-founded recursion in dep-Lambek.

Analytic candidate. Internally a grammar is essentially A : \mathrm {String} \to \mathbb {N} \to \mathbf {Set}, and we could set {\mathopen {}\left (\triangleright A\right )\mathclose {}}\, w\, 0 = \top , \qquad {\mathopen {}\left (\triangleright A\right )\mathclose {}}\, w\, {\mathopen {}\left (\mathsf {suc}\, n\right )\mathclose {}} = A\, w\, n. This is the usual step-indexed later: shift the index by one and give free truth at step zero.

Synthetic candidate. In Agda we could alternatively define {\mathopen {}\left (\triangleright A\right )\mathclose {}}\, w = \triangleright \, {\mathopen {}\left (A\, w\right )\mathclose {}} and inherit the ambient later modality of the synthetic guarded type theory. This keeps grammar-indexing orthogonal to step-indexing.

Open question. Which of these plays best with the Dyck functor / string-decomposition story? The analytic version makes step-indexing and string-length arguments interact explicitly; the synthetic version defers that to the ambient modality but needs to be reconciled with the grammar-as-type-family structure. See also the trivial-case question.

fr:title.text: Trivial case of the guarded modality: should it be top or the current string's quote?

fr:frontmatter.fr:title: Trivial case of the guarded modality: should it be top or the current string's quote?

fr:mainmatter.html:p: Pre-meeting notes for the advisor meeting on 2026-04-22. Branch of guarded modality candidates for Lambek^{D}{}.

The puzzle. In the usual guarded setting, \triangleright A at step 0 gives back \top . But in the Lambek^{D}{} setting we have access to the current string w. I suspect the trivial case should bottom out at \lceil w \rceil rather than \top : {\mathopen {}\left (\triangleright A\right )\mathclose {}}\, w\, 0 \;\stackrel {?}{=}\; \lceil w \rceil . The intuition: at step 0 we've consumed exactly the string w, so the "trivial" proposition is that the string we have is w, not an unconstrained \top .

Tension with the string-decomposition axiom. However, the axiom \top \simeq \mathchoice {\textstyle \oplus _{{\mathopen {}\left (w : \mathrm {String}\right )\mathclose {}}}}{\textstyle \oplus _{{\mathopen {}\left (w : \mathrm {String}\right )\mathclose {}}}}{\scriptstyle \oplus _{{\mathopen {}\left (w : \mathrm {String}\right )\mathclose {}}}}{\scriptscriptstyle \oplus _{{\mathopen {}\left (w : \mathrm {String}\right )\mathclose {}}}}\, \lceil w \rceil (see the Dyck well-foundedness note) already equates \top with a big-\oplus of quotes. Under a fixed w these may collapse: \top restricted to w already is \lceil w \rceil . So the question may be cosmetic — the two presentations might be isomorphic — but the \lceil w \rceil form is likely the one that carries the right definitional equalities for proofs.
To discuss: which form plays better with well-founded recursion and with recursive-descent-as-unfold?

fr:title.text: Subterm ordering and the inverse of the initial algebra as a recursive coalgebra

fr:frontmatter.fr:title: Subterm ordering and the inverse of the initial algebra as a recursive coalgebra

fr:mainmatter.html:p: From the advisor meeting on 2026-04-22. See also well-founded recursion in dep-Lambek and derivative-based CFG parser via recursive coalgebras.

Cass's suggestion. For an initial F-algebra D, there is an evident subterm ordering on D. The inverse of the initial algebra is a coalgebra structure on D, and it might be possible to show that this coalgebra is well-founded with respect to that subterm ordering — obtaining a recursive-coalgebra witness without going through the final coalgebra.

Stronger claim to check. Cass further suggested that the inverse of an initial algebra is always a recursive coalgebra, even when it is not the final coalgebra. The approach rests on this claim, and it needs to be verified — dig into the coalgebra literature (Adámek, Capretta, Uustalu, Vene) for the precise statement.

Why this matters. If true, it gives a categorical justification for recursive definitions on initial algebras like the Dyck grammar without invoking step-indexing or guarded modalities. It would complement — or replace — the guarded-modality candidates as the well-foundedness mechanism.

fr:title.text: Recursive-descent parsers as unfolds

fr:frontmatter.fr:title: Recursive-descent parsers as unfolds

fr:mainmatter.html:p: From the advisor meeting on 2026-04-22.

Max's claim. Recursive-descent parsers cannot be written in a terminating way directly. The fix may be to write them as an unfold (anamorphism / coalgebra map) rather than a fold: the parser is characterised not as a recursive function into a syntax tree, but as a map out of the input stream via a coalgebra structure on the state.

This dovetails with the recursive-coalgebra framing — recursive descent becomes the unique map from the initial/input coalgebra into an F-coalgebra for the grammar's functor. The derivative-based CFG parser plan already walks in this direction.

Concrete takeaway for LL(1). The LL(1) goal (see finishing the deterministic regex code) is the first place to try this: once the grammar functor and its coalgebra-of-derivatives are pinned down, the parser is the unfold, and termination falls out of well-foundedness rather than structural recursion on the input.

fr:title.text: Lexing as morphisms between alphabet literals

fr:frontmatter.fr:title: Lexing as morphisms between alphabet literals

fr:mainmatter.html:p: From the advisor meeting on 2026-04-22. Tangential thought.

The hope. If we allow morphisms between the generating data of Lambek^{D}{} — i.e. between the literals \texttt {"}c\texttt {"} for c : \mathcal {A} — then lexing can be encoded internally: a lexer is just a morphism \texttt {"}c_1\texttt {"} \to \texttt {"}c_2\texttt {"} (or more precisely a morphism between the generated grammars of raw characters and token classes). Traditional categorial grammar does something like this.

Max's pitfall. Having morphisms between generators creates an obligation to be natural with respect to them. That constrains every construction in the calculus and may be a total roadblock — I am unsure.

Possible escape route. There may be an interesting use of tinyness (right adjoints that preserve colimits for size reasons) to escape the naturality obligation in the places that matter. Worth a separate investigation after the core guarded/well-foundedness story stabilises.

fr:title.text: Monadic parser combinators as chains of isos, and the "Dijkstra monad"

fr:frontmatter.fr:title: Monadic parser combinators as chains of isos, and the "Dijkstra monad"

fr:mainmatter.html:p: From the advisor meeting on 2026-04-22. Tangential thought.

Observation. Monadic parser combinators feel like they are naively written via chains of isomorphisms, where each iso relates to the iso between a string and A \oplus \neg A for a complete parser (since a complete parser maps the input into either a grammar A or its complement). This is structurally reminiscent of how quantum languages are forced to invoke chains of isos.

Snag. In the Lambek^{D}{} setting a parser combinator written this naive way cannot be proven terminating directly — the same pathology as recursive descent. But the same escape hatch (well-foundedness via recursive coalgebras or guarded modality) should apply.

The "Dijkstra monad" puzzle. We accumulate complement types as the combinators compose — a sort of negation monad. Ohad called this something like a "Dijkstra monad" a while back. I have not found this nomenclature elsewhere in writing. Action item: ask on Mastodon for the reference.

Apparent step function at depth 4 is "first successful elaboration", not a unifier threshold: Real01–Real03 fail fast with a type-mismatch error because the chain is too short for endpoints to unify (see Open Questions). fr:title.text: Well-foundedness of the Dyck functor via the string-decomposition axiom

fr:frontmatter.fr:title: Well-foundedness of the Dyck functor via the string-decomposition axiom

fr:mainmatter.html:p: Pre-meeting notes for the advisor meeting on 2026-04-22. Context: the well-foundedness sense here is the one in [alexandruIntrinsicallyCorrectAlgorithms2025-preprint], and the tie-in with well-founded recursive coalgebras in dep-Lambek is the reason for caring.
The Dyck functor. Consider the polynomial functor
and let D be its initial F-algebra, so D \simeq I \oplus \texttt {"}lp\texttt {"} \otimes D \otimes \texttt {"}rp\texttt {"} \otimes D.

The string-decomposition axiom. In dep-Lambek we have the axiom \top \simeq \mathchoice {\textstyle \oplus _{{\mathopen {}\left (w : \mathrm {String}\right )\mathclose {}}}}{\textstyle \oplus _{{\mathopen {}\left (w : \mathrm {String}\right )\mathclose {}}}}{\scriptstyle \oplus _{{\mathopen {}\left (w : \mathrm {String}\right )\mathclose {}}}}{\scriptscriptstyle \oplus _{{\mathopen {}\left (w : \mathrm {String}\right )\mathclose {}}}}\, \lceil w \rceil which internalizes the external reasoning on strings: every top-element is quoted as some specific w. Equivalently \top \simeq {\mathtt {Char}}^{*} \quad \text {where} \quad \mathtt {Char} = \mathchoice {\textstyle \oplus _{{\mathopen {}\left (c : \mathcal {A}\right )\mathclose {}}}}{\textstyle \oplus _{{\mathopen {}\left (c : \mathcal {A}\right )\mathclose {}}}}{\scriptstyle \oplus _{{\mathopen {}\left (c : \mathcal {A}\right )\mathclose {}}}}{\scriptscriptstyle \oplus _{{\mathopen {}\left (c : \mathcal {A}\right )\mathclose {}}}}\, \texttt {"}c\texttt {"}.

Decomposing D. Using the axiom we can refine D into an indexed sum over explicit sub-strings. Peeling off one constructor and inserting a quote for each recursive occurrence gives D \simeq I \oplus \mathchoice {\textstyle \oplus _{{\mathopen {}\left (w : \mathrm {String}\right )\mathclose {}}}}{\textstyle \oplus _{{\mathopen {}\left (w : \mathrm {String}\right )\mathclose {}}}}{\scriptstyle \oplus _{{\mathopen {}\left (w : \mathrm {String}\right )\mathclose {}}}}{\scriptscriptstyle \oplus _{{\mathopen {}\left (w : \mathrm {String}\right )\mathclose {}}}}\, \mathchoice {\textstyle \oplus _{{\mathopen {}\left ({\mathopen {}\left (w = \texttt {"}lp\texttt {"}\, w_1\, \texttt {"}rp\texttt {"}\, w_2\right )\mathclose {}}\right )\mathclose {}}}}{\textstyle \oplus _{{\mathopen {}\left ({\mathopen {}\left (w = \texttt {"}lp\texttt {"}\, w_1\, \texttt {"}rp\texttt {"}\, w_2\right )\mathclose {}}\right )\mathclose {}}}}{\scriptstyle \oplus _{{\mathopen {}\left ({\mathopen {}\left (w = \texttt {"}lp\texttt {"}\, w_1\, \texttt {"}rp\texttt {"}\, w_2\right )\mathclose {}}\right )\mathclose {}}}}{\scriptscriptstyle \oplus _{{\mathopen {}\left ({\mathopen {}\left (w = \texttt {"}lp\texttt {"}\, w_1\, \texttt {"}rp\texttt {"}\, w_2\right )\mathclose {}}\right )\mathclose {}}}}\, \texttt {"}lp\texttt {"} \otimes {\mathopen {}\left (\lceil w_1 \rceil \mathrel {\And } D\right )\mathclose {}} \otimes \texttt {"}rp\texttt {"} \otimes {\mathopen {}\left (\lceil w_2 \rceil \mathrel {\And } D\right )\mathclose {}}.

Because w = \texttt {"}lp\texttt {"}\, w_1\, \texttt {"}rp\texttt {"}\, w_2, we know |w_1|, |w_2| < |w|. The well-foundedness argument is now visible in the type: the recursive D occurrences are guarded by shorter quoted strings.

Reading. The string-decomposition axiom is doing all of the work of externally reasoning about string length. Everything that normally lives "on paper" — inducting on |w|, case-splitting on the first character — is now accessible internally through the quote types \lceil - \rceil and the \oplus /\mathrel {\And } structure. See also the trivial-case question for the related \top vs. \lceil w \rceil puzzle in the guarded setting.

fr:title.text: Candidates for a guarded modality in dep-Lambek

fr:frontmatter.fr:title: Candidates for a guarded modality in dep-Lambek

fr:mainmatter.html:p: Pre-meeting notes for the advisor meeting on 2026-04-22. Related: Can I use guarded recursion?, well-founded recursion in dep-Lambek.

Analytic candidate. Internally a grammar is essentially A : \mathrm {String} \to \mathbb {N} \to \mathbf {Set}, and we could set {\mathopen {}\left (\triangleright A\right )\mathclose {}}\, w\, 0 = \top , \qquad {\mathopen {}\left (\triangleright A\right )\mathclose {}}\, w\, {\mathopen {}\left (\mathsf {suc}\, n\right )\mathclose {}} = A\, w\, n. This is the usual step-indexed later: shift the index by one and give free truth at step zero.

Synthetic candidate. In Agda we could alternatively define {\mathopen {}\left (\triangleright A\right )\mathclose {}}\, w = \triangleright \, {\mathopen {}\left (A\, w\right )\mathclose {}} and inherit the ambient later modality of the synthetic guarded type theory. This keeps grammar-indexing orthogonal to step-indexing.

Open question. Which of these plays best with the Dyck functor / string-decomposition story? The analytic version makes step-indexing and string-length arguments interact explicitly; the synthetic version defers that to the ambient modality but needs to be reconciled with the grammar-as-type-family structure. See also the trivial-case question.

fr:title.text: Trivial case of the guarded modality: should it be top or the current string's quote?

fr:frontmatter.fr:title: Trivial case of the guarded modality: should it be top or the current string's quote?

fr:mainmatter.html:p: Pre-meeting notes for the advisor meeting on 2026-04-22. Branch of guarded modality candidates for Lambek^{D}{}.

The puzzle. In the usual guarded setting, \triangleright A at step 0 gives back \top . But in the Lambek^{D}{} setting we have access to the current string w. I suspect the trivial case should bottom out at \lceil w \rceil rather than \top : {\mathopen {}\left (\triangleright A\right )\mathclose {}}\, w\, 0 \;\stackrel {?}{=}\; \lceil w \rceil . The intuition: at step 0 we've consumed exactly the string w, so the "trivial" proposition is that the string we have is w, not an unconstrained \top .

Tension with the string-decomposition axiom. However, the axiom \top \simeq \mathchoice {\textstyle \oplus _{{\mathopen {}\left (w : \mathrm {String}\right )\mathclose {}}}}{\textstyle \oplus _{{\mathopen {}\left (w : \mathrm {String}\right )\mathclose {}}}}{\scriptstyle \oplus _{{\mathopen {}\left (w : \mathrm {String}\right )\mathclose {}}}}{\scriptscriptstyle \oplus _{{\mathopen {}\left (w : \mathrm {String}\right )\mathclose {}}}}\, \lceil w \rceil (see the Dyck well-foundedness note) already equates \top with a big-\oplus of quotes. Under a fixed w these may collapse: \top restricted to w already is \lceil w \rceil . So the question may be cosmetic — the two presentations might be isomorphic — but the \lceil w \rceil form is likely the one that carries the right definitional equalities for proofs.
To discuss: which form plays better with well-founded recursion and with recursive-descent-as-unfold?

fr:title.text: Subterm ordering and the inverse of the initial algebra as a recursive coalgebra

fr:frontmatter.fr:title: Subterm ordering and the inverse of the initial algebra as a recursive coalgebra

fr:mainmatter.html:p: From the advisor meeting on 2026-04-22. See also well-founded recursion in dep-Lambek and derivative-based CFG parser via recursive coalgebras.

Cass's suggestion. For an initial F-algebra D, there is an evident subterm ordering on D. The inverse of the initial algebra is a coalgebra structure on D, and it might be possible to show that this coalgebra is well-founded with respect to that subterm ordering — obtaining a recursive-coalgebra witness without going through the final coalgebra.

Stronger claim to check. Cass further suggested that the inverse of an initial algebra is always a recursive coalgebra, even when it is not the final coalgebra. The approach rests on this claim, and it needs to be verified — dig into the coalgebra literature (Adámek, Capretta, Uustalu, Vene) for the precise statement.

Why this matters. If true, it gives a categorical justification for recursive definitions on initial algebras like the Dyck grammar without invoking step-indexing or guarded modalities. It would complement — or replace — the guarded-modality candidates as the well-foundedness mechanism.

fr:title.text: Recursive-descent parsers as unfolds

fr:frontmatter.fr:title: Recursive-descent parsers as unfolds

fr:mainmatter.html:p: From the advisor meeting on 2026-04-22.

Max's claim. Recursive-descent parsers cannot be written in a terminating way directly. The fix may be to write them as an unfold (anamorphism / coalgebra map) rather than a fold: the parser is characterised not as a recursive function into a syntax tree, but as a map out of the input stream via a coalgebra structure on the state.

This dovetails with the recursive-coalgebra framing — recursive descent becomes the unique map from the initial/input coalgebra into an F-coalgebra for the grammar's functor. The derivative-based CFG parser plan already walks in this direction.

Concrete takeaway for LL(1). The LL(1) goal (see finishing the deterministic regex code) is the first place to try this: once the grammar functor and its coalgebra-of-derivatives are pinned down, the parser is the unfold, and termination falls out of well-foundedness rather than structural recursion on the input.

fr:title.text: Lexing as morphisms between alphabet literals

fr:frontmatter.fr:title: Lexing as morphisms between alphabet literals

fr:mainmatter.html:p: From the advisor meeting on 2026-04-22. Tangential thought.

The hope. If we allow morphisms between the generating data of Lambek^{D}{} — i.e. between the literals \texttt {"}c\texttt {"} for c : \mathcal {A} — then lexing can be encoded internally: a lexer is just a morphism \texttt {"}c_1\texttt {"} \to \texttt {"}c_2\texttt {"} (or more precisely a morphism between the generated grammars of raw characters and token classes). Traditional categorial grammar does something like this.

Max's pitfall. Having morphisms between generators creates an obligation to be natural with respect to them. That constrains every construction in the calculus and may be a total roadblock — I am unsure.

Possible escape route. There may be an interesting use of tinyness (right adjoints that preserve colimits for size reasons) to escape the naturality obligation in the places that matter. Worth a separate investigation after the core guarded/well-foundedness story stabilises.

fr:title.text: Monadic parser combinators as chains of isos, and the "Dijkstra monad"

fr:frontmatter.fr:title: Monadic parser combinators as chains of isos, and the "Dijkstra monad"

fr:mainmatter.html:p: From the advisor meeting on 2026-04-22. Tangential thought.

Observation. Monadic parser combinators feel like they are naively written via chains of isomorphisms, where each iso relates to the iso between a string and A \oplus \neg A for a complete parser (since a complete parser maps the input into either a grammar A or its complement). This is structurally reminiscent of how quantum languages are forced to invoke chains of isos.

Snag. In the Lambek^{D}{} setting a parser combinator written this naive way cannot be proven terminating directly — the same pathology as recursive descent. But the same escape hatch (well-foundedness via recursive coalgebras or guarded modality) should apply.

The "Dijkstra monad" puzzle. We accumulate complement types as the combinators compose — a sort of negation monad. Ohad called this something like a "Dijkstra monad" a while back. I have not found this nomenclature elsewhere in writing. Action item: ask on Mastodon for the reference.

fr:title.text: Lean Implementation of Dependent Lambek Calculus

fr:frontmatter.fr:title: Lean Implementation of Dependent Lambek Calculus

fr:mainmatter.html:p: Goal: a Lean 4 implementation of Dependent Lambek Calculus whose surface syntax mirrors the on-paper presentation and elaborates, via Lean's extensible elaboration and metaprogramming, into the denotational semantics. The implementation should faithfully realize the full linear / non-linear calculus and be generic enough to evaluate the syntax in any category with sufficient structure — not solely the category of grammars.

Starting point. A Claude-written sketch lives in ~/grammars-and-semantic-actions/Lean/ (root LambekD.lean, elaborator under LambekD/Elab/, ~3.7k lines). It compiles and has working [| ... |] elaboration for the ordered linear fragment plus a grammar_inductive command. It is unaudited: the syntax/semantics correspondence and the design of the elaborator are not yet fully understood or owned. Treat it as scaffolding, not as a finished implementation.

html:ul.html:li: An elaboration pipeline from the on-paper Lambek^D syntax into Lean terms that I understand end-to-end and can extend.
An embedded DSL for the full linear / non-linear calculus (not just the ordered linear fragment).

An abstraction of the elaborator over the target category, so that the same surface syntax can be interpreted in any sufficiently structured category — recovering the grammars instance as one example.

fr:title.text: How the LinearElab Elaborator Compiles to Category-Polymorphic Morphisms

fr:frontmatter.fr:title: How the LinearElab Elaborator Compiles to Category-Polymorphic Morphisms

fr:mainmatter.html:p: Intuitive walkthrough of Lean/LambekD/LinearElab/ — how a surface term like

gets turned into a morphism \llbracket {A \otimes B}\rrbracket _\ell \to A \otimes B in an abstract monoidal / biclosed / (co)cartesian / indexed / inductive category \mathcal {C}. Meant to be read alongside the code, not as a spec.

fr:title.text: The big picture

fr:frontmatter.fr:title: The big picture

fr:mainmatter.html:p: The elaborator is a syntax-to-syntax preprocessor. It does not manufacture Lean Exprs itself; instead it reads a DSL expression, decides for each subterm which typed combinator should stand in for it, and builds a Lean source-level term that applies those combinators. The generated source is handed back to Lean's normal elabTerm at the very end. Unification, typeclass resolution, and universe inference happen once, there, on the full tree — not piecewise while we are walking the DSL.
Conceptually:

html:ul.html:li: DSL syntax (category lterm) lives in LinearElab/Syntax.lean. Each connective of the paper has its own shape: (x, y), let (a,b) = _ in _, fun (x:A) =>, ⟨e₁, e₂⟩, match _ with | inl a => _ | inr b => _, and so on.

Combinators live in LambekD.Linear.{Monoidal,Biclosed, Cartesian,Cocartesian,IndexedProducts,IndexedCoproducts,Inductive}. Each is a plain Lean definition parametric in a category \mathcal {C} carrying only the structure that connective needs (monoidal, left- closed, right-closed, chosen products, chosen coproducts, chosen distributor, initial algebras). No reference to Grammar.

The elaborator in LinearElab/Elaborator.lean is the bridge: one partial def per DSL form, emitting a TSyntax `term that mentions exactly the right combinator with exactly the right context arguments pinned down.

fr:title.text: What the combinators want from us

fr:frontmatter.fr:title: What the combinators want from us

fr:mainmatter.html:p: Take tensorIntro as representative:
tensorIntro (e₁ : ⟦Δ⟧ₗ ⟶ A) (e₂ : ⟦Δ'⟧ₗ ⟶ B) : ⟦Δ ++ Δ'⟧ₗ ⟶ A ⊗ B (with Δ, Δ', A, B implicit).

LinCtx C is an ordered left-to-right list of \mathcal {C}-objects (think: a telescope of linear types). ⟦_⟧ₗ folds it into a right-nested tensor. The combinator takes two morphisms, on contexts Δ and Δ', and returns a morphism on the concatenated context Δ ++ Δ'.

So when the user writes (e₁, e₂) with ambient context \Delta _{\text {full}}, there is exactly one decision to make: where to cut \Delta _{\text {full}} into a prefix \Delta used by e₁ and a suffix \Delta ' used by e₂. The rest — what A, B, and \mathcal {C} are — is Lean's problem.

Every other combinator is the same pattern. Some take one context (var, unitIntro, prodIntro, sumInl); some take a middle slice and an outer prefix + suffix (unitElim, tensorElim, sumElim, coprodDElim, botElim); the rest are binders that add or remove a single slot at the front or the end (limpRIntro, limpLIntro, funD). The elaborator's job is to look at the DSL shape, compute the cuts, and emit the corresponding combinator applied to its inputs with the cuts threaded through explicitly.

fr:title.text: The cutting algorithm: free variables and ordering

fr:frontmatter.fr:title: The cutting algorithm: free variables and ordering

fr:mainmatter.html:p: Two tiny helpers do almost all the work.

html:ul.html:li: freeVars : TSyntax `lterm → Array Name — purely syntactic, recurses through the term and collects identifiers that are not shadowed by a binder. It knows about all the DSL's binding forms (let () = _ in, let (a,b) = _ in, fun (x:T) =>, funl (x:T) =>, match _ with | inl a | inr b, matchD _ with | ⟪x, y⟫).

splitCtx fvLeft fvRight — walks the ambient context left-to-right and finds the unique split point i such that the first i names lie in fvLeft and the rest in fvRight. Throws an error if any variable is unused, reused across branches, or appears out of order.

fr:mainmatter.html:p: For middle-slice forms (let (a,b) = e in e' and friends) there is a second helper splitCtxMiddle fvMid fvOuter that finds a contiguous range of indices all of whose variables lie in fvMid, asserts that range really is contiguous, and returns the three pieces \Delta '_1, \Delta , \Delta '_2 around it.

These two functions enforce ordered linearity — no contraction (variable appearing twice on the same side of a split), no weakening (a variable that goes nowhere), no exchange (a left-variable appearing after a right-variable). When the user-written binder structure of the DSL does not support a valid cut, splitCtx itself raises the error. The main loop never has to think about linearity; it only asks "where does the cut go?" and delegates.

Cartesian and indexed-product intro are the only forms that do not cut: ⟨e₁, e₂⟩ shares the whole ambient context between the two branches (cartesian is additive, so it permits the same resources to be used by both). The elaborator simply recurses on each branch with the full ctx and lets the branches' internal linearity checks enforce that each branch really does consume it.

fr:title.text: The unification subtlety — why we pin Δ with named arguments

fr:frontmatter.fr:title: The unification subtlety — why we pin Δ with named arguments

fr:mainmatter.html:p: Combinators like tensorIntro type as ⟦Δ ++ Δ'⟧ₗ ⟶ A ⊗ B. When we apply such a combinator to a concrete ambient context \Delta _{\text {full}}, Lean's unifier tries to solve Δ ++ Δ' = Δ_full. That equation has many solutions (any cut point works), and because LinCtx.append recurses on its right argument, Lean's unifier eagerly pins \Delta ' to some small suffix and leaves \Delta as whatever is left — typically not the split our FV analysis computed.
To stop Lean from guessing, the elaborator serialises the exact cut pieces back into surface syntax:

html:p.html:code: ctxToSyntax vars = nil.snoc A₀.snoc A₁. ⋯ .snoc A_k

fr:mainmatter.html:p: and passes them to the combinator as named implicit arguments ((Δ := $Δstx) / (Δ' := $Δ'stx)). Now when Lean sees tensorIntro (Δ := A,B) (Δ' := C,D) m₁ m₂, both halves are syntactically pinned and the equation (A,B) ++ (C,D) = A,B,C,D reduces definitionally. No unification ambiguity remains.
The same trick is what unblocks middle-slice combinators (unitElim, tensorElim, sumElim, coprodDElim, botElim), which have two append patterns in their types.

fr:title.text: Per-connective intuitions

fr:frontmatter.fr:title: Per-connective intuitions

fr:title.text: Monoidal (the skeleton)

fr:frontmatter.fr:title: Monoidal (the skeleton)

fr:mainmatter.html:p: x ⟶ Linear.var A: singleton context [(x, A)] maps by identity into the slot.
() ⟶ Linear.unitIntro: requires empty context, produces the monoidal unit I.
(e₁, e₂) ⟶ tensorIntro (Δ := …) (Δ' := …) m₁ m₂: splitCtx (FV e₁) (FV e₂) picks the cut; each branch is elaborated in its own piece of the context.

let () = e in e' and let (a,b) = e in e': e consumes a middle slice Δ, e' runs on Δ'₁ ++ Δ'₂ (plus the new binders in the pair case). We emit unitElim / tensorElim with the three pieces pinned. The new binders in the pair case get hole types _; Lean fills them from the type of e.

fr:title.text: Biclosed (binders)

fr:frontmatter.fr:title: Biclosed (binders)

fr:mainmatter.html:p: Ordinary functions come in two flavours because context is ordered. fun (x : A) => e pushes x onto the end of the ambient ctx and emits limpRIntro (Δ := ambient) body, producing A →[C] B. funl (x : A) => e pushes it onto the front and emits limpLIntro (Δ := ambient) body, producing B [C]← A. The ambient ctx is passed as Δ so that Lean does not try to solve Δ.snoc A = newCtx or sole A ++ Δ = newCtx by guessing.

Application likewise splits into two rules by which side the function appears on. f a (juxtaposition, function on the left) is limpRApp; a ·⟜ f (argument on the left) is limpLApp. The two combinators have their append patterns in opposite orders (Δ ++ Δ' vs Δ' ++ Δ), so the elaborator has to know which side is the function when it emits the call.

fr:title.text: Cartesian (⟨⟩, ⟨e₁, e₂⟩, π₁, π₂)

fr:frontmatter.fr:title: Cartesian (⟨⟩, ⟨e₁, e₂⟩, π₁, π₂)

fr:mainmatter.html:p: Additive, so there is no cut: ⟨e₁, e₂⟩ elaborates both branches under the same ambient context, and Lean's A \amp B constructor uses the cartesian lift combinator. ⟨⟩ is the unique morphism into the chosen terminal and accepts any ambient ctx. Projections just post-compose with fst or snd.

fr:title.text: Cocartesian (inl, inr, match, absurd)

fr:frontmatter.fr:title: Cocartesian (inl, inr, match, absurd)

fr:mainmatter.html:p: Injections are pre-composed with inl / inr — no cut.

match e with | inl a => f | inr b => g is the only genuinely subtle monoidal case outside tensor-elim. The scrutinee e consumes a contiguous middle slice \Delta , and both branches share the outer context \Delta '_1, \Delta '_2, each extending it with one new binder (a or b, with hole types filled from e's type). Emission is sumElim (Δ'₁ := …) (Δ := …) (Δ'₂ := …) m mf mg; the underlying combinator bakes in the distributor so that the two branches of the coproduct really do glue back into a single morphism on the whole ambient ctx.

absurd e is \bot -elim. The scrutinee provides a morphism into the initial object; the distributor's annihilation maps any flanking context to the initial. That means we are allowed to have ambient variables that do not appear in e at all — they just get annihilated. In freeVars this breaks the usual "every variable must be used somewhere" invariant, so the elaborator special-cases absurd: ambient vars outside FV(e) are treated as "used by the annihilation", not as an unused-variable error.

fr:title.text: Indexed products and coproducts (non-linear binders)

fr:frontmatter.fr:title: Indexed products and coproducts (non-linear binders)

fr:mainmatter.html:p: funD (x : X) => e introduces a non-linear (Lean-level) binder x : X that the body can mention as an ordinary Lean term but not as a linear variable. The linear context is unchanged for the body — nothing is consumed. The elaborator elaborates e under the same ambient ctx, then wraps the result in a Lean fun x : X => _ and hands that to prodDIntro, which is exactly the liftD of the chosen indexed-product structure.
e ·@ x post-composes the projection at index x.
⟪x, e⟫ injects at a specified index; coprodDInj x e.

matchD e with | ⟪x, y⟫ => body: like match, e consumes a middle slice and body gets one new linear binder y (with a hole type inferred from the index family) and one non-linear binder x : X. Emission is coprodDElim (Δ'₁ := …) (Δ := …) (Δ'₂ := …) m (fun x => body), where the fun x => … captures the non-linear binder from the surface syntax.

fr:title.text: Initial algebras (roll, fold)

fr:frontmatter.fr:title: Initial algebras (roll, fold)

fr:mainmatter.html:p: roll[x] e is muRoll _ x e, which is literally e ≫ HasInitialAlgebra.roll x: post-compose the linear body with the initial algebra's constructor at index x. The _ is a placeholder for the functor F, which Lean is expected to recover from the expected return type \mu F x.

fold[algs] e is muFold algs e = e ≫ HasInitialAlgebra.fold algs x: post-compose with the catamorphism induced by the algebra algs : ∀ y, (F y).denote A ⟶ A y. roll and fold do not restructure the context; they just chain on top of it.

The \beta and \eta laws of initial algebras (fold_roll, fold_unique) are semantic lemmas, not judgmental — the elaborator does nothing to expose them, it is up to the programmer to rewrite when needed.

fr:title.text: Entry point: the DSL brackets

fr:frontmatter.fr:title: Entry point: the DSL brackets

fr:mainmatter.html:p: The top-level macro in elabLinearBracket:

html:ol.html:li: Reads the surface syntax (x₁ : A₁) … (xₙ : Aₙ) => body.
Builds the initial ElabCtx from the typed binders: an array of (Name × TSyntax `term) pairs, in the order written.

Runs the elaborator elabLTerm body under that context. The output is a single TSyntax `term — a Lean source-level term mentioning Linear.tensorIntro, Linear.sumElim, etc., with all context pieces and non-linear binders wired up.

Calls Lean.Elab.Term.elabTerm on that syntax with the expected type from the surrounding Lean context. Unification and typeclass resolution — for the category \mathcal {C} itself, for the types of the binders, for the appropriate chosen-structure instances — all happen here, once, on the finished tree.

fr:mainmatter.html:p: The elaborator never inspects Expr, never calls isDefEq, never synthesises an instance. It is a syntactic preprocessor that knows how to name the right combinators and pin their context implicits; everything semantic is Lean's job.

fr:title.text: What is not there (yet)

fr:frontmatter.fr:title: What is not there (yet)

html:ul.html:li: No escape hatch #[f] to embed a Lean-level morphism. The grammar-specific Elab/ elaborator has one; the linear one does not — if you need to use a Lean-constructed morphism, you must currently write the term directly (as in the prodDIntro smoke test which falls back to the raw combinator).
No constructor-apps for grammar_inductive-style named data. The inductive surface here is only the roll/fold pair.
No match … with on μ F beyond what fold expresses, and no equivalent of the grammar_decreasing termination plumbing. Both were grammar-specific in the older elaborator.
No Lean-level rewrite / simp hooks; β/η laws of each connective exist as simp lemmas on the combinators, but the DSL does not surface them.

fr:mainmatter.html:p: These are all deliberate omissions — the LinearElab elaborator is the minimal, category-polymorphic core. The grammar-specific pieces live in the older Elab/ tree and compose with these combinators via instances on Grammar.
